title: Juniors and parents: support without pressure
summary: The coach teaches, the parent supports. Praise effort and the routine rather than the score, let the child start the talk afterwards, and stay quiet behind the stand.

body.html: A child shoots because it is interesting and fun, and the parents' job is to protect that. Technique is the coach's job: two voices with different advice confuse a child. If something worries you, talk to the coach in private, not on the stand.

Studies of youth sport in general suggest that children keep enjoying their sport when parents let them make their own choices. It also helps when parents are involved but not too much, and care more about learning than about winning. Few of these studies are about shooting, so most likely this applies to clay shooting too.

Praise effort and the routine, not only hits: that the child ran the pre-shot routine calmly, handled the gun safely and kept going after misses. Set process goals, such as “my routine on each target”, rather than “20 of 25”.

Nerves before a competition are normal. Help with simple things: sleep, breakfast, arriving early, packing kit without a rush. “You have to win” adds pressure; “shoot like in training, I'm proud of you” can ease it.
After a round, do not go over mistakes straight away. Let the child start the conversation, listen, and give them time to cool down. Going over the round is the coach's job, once the child is ready.
Show the same warmth after a good round and a bad one. Your love and support should not depend on the score.
Compare the child with their own past, not with others. Over a season, the results in their shooter profile on ClayArena can show the progress. A bad day is part of learning, not a verdict.

During a competition, nobody may coach a competitor. Tips from behind the stand can earn the child a yellow card, and the referee sends the person giving them out of the shooting area (Chapter 8 · No coaching during competition, Chapter 21 · No coaching during competition).

Do not comment on referee decisions either. In Compak® Sporting, shooters or spectators who openly criticise a decision without the referee's permission can face jury sanctions as an attempt to influence the referee (Chapter 22 · What counts as an attempt to influence). In Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ this rule names the shooters (Chapter 11 · What counts as influencing the referee). Either way, support quietly, with a smile and your presence.

Watch for signs of burnout: the child no longer wants to go to the ground, or gets angry at each miss. A break, or time for another sport, can help. Interest that returns by itself is stronger than pressure.
If a child's anxiety stays high for weeks or affects sleep or school, talk to the coach and consider a sport psychologist or a doctor.

notes.html: Agree with the parents who gives technical advice: one voice, the coach's. Before a competition, tell them where they may stand and remind them of the coaching rule.

key_points.html: The coach teaches technique; parents support.
Praise effort and the routine, not the score.
Let the child start the talk after a round.
No tips from behind the stand and no comments on referee decisions.
The same warmth after a good round and a bad one.

did_you_know.html: Some youth shooting programmes ask parents to focus on what the child learns along the way, while the coach and the child work on results.

quiz.q: Who should explain shooting technique to the child?
quiz.explain: One voice, the coach's, does not confuse the child; the parents support.

quiz.q: Which goal is a process goal?
quiz.explain: A process goal is about what the child controls, not about the final score.

quiz.q: May a parent give tips from behind the stand during a competition?
quiz.explain: Coaching during a competition can earn the child a yellow card, and the person coaching is sent away.
